findings.summary: The SAVEPOINT example calls RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp2 after rolling back past it, which is an error because sp2 no longer exists.
findings.evidence: "ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;","RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp2;" — PostgreSQL docs: "ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT implicitly destroys all savepoints that were established after the named savepoint"; MySQL: "All savepoints of the current transaction that were set after the named savepoint was set are deleted" and RELEASE of a missing savepoint raises ERROR 1305 (42000): SAVEPOINT sp2 does not exist.
findings.fix: Drop the final `RELEASE SAVEPOINT sp2;` line (or move it before the `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;`), and add a note that rolling back to sp1 automatically discards sp2.

findings.summary: The note on the SAVEPOINT example wrongly implies only the work after sp2 is undone, when everything after sp1 is rolled back.
findings.evidence: lines "SAVEPOINT sp1;","-- some operations","SAVEPOINT sp2;","-- more operations","ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT sp1;" with note "sp2 work is undone, sp1 work stays" — but "-- some operations" ran after sp1 and is also undone; the page's own callout says rollback undoes "changes made after that point only".
findings.fix: Change the note to "everything after sp1 is undone (both blocks of operations); only work done before sp1 survives".

findings.summary: The 5NF example states a rule ("any two columns together determine the third") that is a functional dependency, not a join dependency, and is contradicted by the example's own data.
findings.evidence: "Example: SPJ(Supplier, Part, Project), JD *(SP, SJ, PJ)","any two columns together determine the third" — yet the SP/SJ/PJ tables join to {(S1,P1,J1),(S1,P1,J2),(S1,P2,J1),(S2,P1,J1)}, where (S1,P1) maps to both J1 and J2, so (Supplier,Part) does not determine Project.
findings.fix: Replace the line with the actual join-dependency rule: "if (s,p) appears in SP, (p,j) in PJ and (s,j) in SJ, then (s,p,j) must appear in SPJ" — note that no pair functionally determines the third attribute (if one did, the relation would decompose by FDs instead).

findings.summary: The TEACHING relation given as a BCNF example is actually a 2NF violation with a single candidate key, so it does not illustrate BCNF or overlapping candidate keys.
findings.evidence: "fixes anomalies from **overlapping candidate keys**","Example: TEACHING(Teacher_ID, Course_ID, Course_Name), key = both","FD Course_ID → Course_Name" — Course_ID is part of the only candidate key (Teacher_ID, Course_ID), so Course_ID → Course_Name is a partial dependency that breaks 2NF, and there is only one candidate key to overlap; the later table caption repeats this as "anomalies due to multiple candidate keys".
findings.fix: Use a genuine 3NF-but-not-BCNF example with overlapping candidate keys, e.g. TEACHES(Student, Subject, Teacher) with candidate keys {Student, Subject} and {Student, Teacher} and FD Teacher → Subject; or relabel the current example as a 2NF/partial-dependency illustration.

findings.summary: The blanket claim that SQL is not case sensitive is wrong for identifiers and string data in most engines.
findings.evidence: "not case sensitive, but written in **UPPERCASE** by convention" — only keywords are case-insensitive; PostgreSQL folds unquoted identifiers to lower case and treats quoted ones as case-sensitive, and string comparisons are case-sensitive under most collations.
findings.fix: Rewrite as "SQL **keywords** are case-insensitive; identifiers and stored string values may be case-sensitive depending on the DBMS and collation".
